position: both — after a verb it is usually written without hyphens: *the suit was made to order*

senses.gloss: Made specially for one customer instead of in standard sizes.
examples: He wears *made-to-order* shirts from a little shop downtown.
The cabinets are *made-to-order*, so delivery takes six weeks.
A *made-to-order* sofa costs twice as much as one off the floor.

form: compound — from the phrasal verb *make up*
contrast: As a verb the two words stay apart: *she made up the whole story*.

senses.gloss: Invented, not true or not real.
examples: That's a *made-up* word — you won't find it in any dictionary.
He told his boss a *made-up* story about a flat tire.
The names in the book are all *made-up*.

senses.gloss: Wearing makeup.
examples: She arrived heavily *made-up* for the photo shoot.
His face was *made-up* to look forty years older.

senses.gloss: Of a bright purplish pink.
examples: She painted the front door *magenta*.
The printer is out of *magenta* ink.
A row of *magenta* flowers ran along the fence.

position: attributive only — after a verb use *magical*: *the evening was magical*
contrast: *Magic* names the thing itself (*a magic wand*); *magical* describes how something feels (*a magical evening*). *Magic* is also a noun.

senses.gloss: Using or produced by supernatural power.
examples: He pulled a rabbit out of a hat — the oldest *magic* trick there is.
In the story a *magic* mirror answers every question.

senses.gloss: Working so well that it seems impossible.
examples: There is no *magic* formula for losing weight.
Her *magic* touch with angry customers saved the store.

senses.gloss: So beautiful or happy that it feels like magic.
examples: Venice in the fog was *magical*.
They spent a *magical* week on the coast.

senses.gloss: Of magic, or having magic powers.
examples: The ring is said to have *magical* properties.
He studies *magical* beliefs in medieval Europe.

senses.gloss: Generous and forgiving, especially toward someone you have beaten.
examples: The champion was *magnanimous* in victory and praised her opponent.
It was a *magnanimous* gesture to pay for everyone's dinner.
He could have sued, but he chose to be *magnanimous*.

senses.gloss: Of a magnet, or acting like one.
examples: The compass needle follows the Earth's *magnetic* field.
The knives hang on a *magnetic* strip above the counter.

senses.gloss: So attractive that people cannot look away.
examples: She has a *magnetic* presence on stage.
His *magnetic* personality filled the room.

senses.gloss: Made to act like a magnet.
examples: Rub the needle on a magnet until it is *magnetized*.
The screwdriver has a *magnetized* tip so screws don't fall.
Keep the card away from anything *magnetized*.

senses.gloss: Extremely impressive in size, beauty or quality.
examples: The view from the ridge was *magnificent*.
She gave a *magnificent* performance in the second act.
They restored the old theater to its *magnificent* original state.

senses.gloss: Grand and dignified enough to command respect.
examples: A *majestic* elk stepped out of the trees.
The cathedral looks *majestic* from the river.
The organ opened with a slow, *majestic* chord.

position: attributive only — for *the problem is big* English does not say *the problem is major*

senses.gloss: Large or important, more so than the others.
examples: Traffic is a *major* problem downtown.
She played a *major* role in the merger.
The storm did *major* damage to the pier.

senses.gloss: In music, of the scale that sounds bright rather than sad.
examples: The piece is in C *major*.
He switched from a minor key to a *major* one for the chorus.

contrast: Also a noun: *a world of make-believe*.

senses.gloss: Existing only in play or imagination.
examples: The kids served us *make-believe* tea in plastic cups.
He grew up in a *make-believe* world of knights and dragons.
It was a *make-believe* store with cardboard shelves.

senses.gloss: Put together quickly out of whatever was at hand, as a temporary fix.
examples: They built a *makeshift* shelter out of tarps and rope.
The gym became a *makeshift* hospital during the flood.
A crate served as a *makeshift* table.

senses.gloss: Unable to fit in with other people or with normal life.
examples: The school takes in kids other districts call *maladjusted*.
He was lonely and *maladjusted* his whole first year.
Years abroad left her *maladjusted* to small-town life.

contrast: Always capitalized. *A Malaysian* is the noun for a person.

senses.gloss: Of Malaysia or its people.
examples: We ate at a *Malaysian* restaurant near the station.
The team's coach is *Malaysian*.
She studies *Malaysian* trade policy.

contrast: *Male* is about sex; *masculine* is about qualities felt to belong to men. Also a noun: *the males of the species*.

senses.gloss: Of the sex that fathers young; of men and boys.
examples: A *male* lion can weigh four hundred pounds.
Most of the applicants were *male*.
The clinic offers a *male* nurse on every shift.

senses.gloss: Of a plug or part that fits into another.
examples: You need a cable with a *male* connector on both ends.
The *male* end goes into the wall socket.

senses.gloss: Wanting to do harm to other people.
examples: The novel's villain is quietly *malevolent*.
She gave him a *malevolent* stare across the table.
Nothing in his face was *malevolent*, only tired.

senses.gloss: Shaped wrongly, usually from birth or from a fault in making.
examples: The puppy was born with a *malformed* paw.
A *malformed* valve caused the leak.
Several of the seedlings came up *malformed*.

senses.gloss: Not working the way it should.
examples: A *malfunctioning* sensor shut the whole line down.
The elevator has been *malfunctioning* since Tuesday.
They traced the fire to a *malfunctioning* space heater.

senses.gloss: Meant to hurt someone, and done on purpose.
examples: He was charged with *malicious* damage to property.
Someone spread a *malicious* rumor about her.
The email carried *malicious* software.

contrast: Also a verb with the same sound — *to malign someone* is to say evil things about them. For illness use *malignant*.

senses.gloss: Harmful in a quiet, lasting way.
examples: Money had a *malign* influence on the whole election.
He blamed the crash on the *malign* neglect of the regulators.
The war left a *malign* mark on two generations.

senses.gloss: Of a tumor: cancerous and likely to spread.
examples: The biopsy showed the growth was *malignant*.
Doctors removed the *malignant* tissue last week.

senses.gloss: Full of hatred and wanting to do harm.
examples: There was something *malignant* in the way he smiled.
The city fought a *malignant* rumor for months.

senses.gloss: Of metal: soft enough to be hammered or pressed into shape.
examples: Gold is the most *malleable* of all metals.
Heat the copper until it turns *malleable*.

senses.gloss: Of a person: easily influenced or changed.
examples: New recruits are young and *malleable*.
He wanted a *malleable* deputy, not one with opinions.

senses.gloss: Weak and unhealthy from not getting enough good food.
examples: The dog was *malnourished* when the shelter took it in.
One child in five in the region is *malnourished*.
He treated *malnourished* patients for two years in the camp.

contrast: Formal or joking. Everyday American English says *smelly*.

senses.gloss: Smelling very bad.
examples: A *malodorous* pile of trash sat by the loading dock.
The locker room was warm and *malodorous*.
He opened a *malodorous* container from the back of the fridge.

senses.gloss: Made from grain that has been soaked and dried to bring out its sugar.
examples: He ordered a *malted* milkshake.
The recipe calls for two cups of *malted* barley.
*Malted* milk powder gives the cookies their flavor.

contrast: Always capitalized. The same form serves for one person and for many: *two Maltese sailors*.

senses.gloss: Of Malta, its people or its language.
examples: *Maltese* is the only Semitic language written in the Latin alphabet.
She married a *Maltese* engineer.
The harbor is lined with *Maltese* fishing boats.

senses.gloss: Of mammals.
examples: Whales share the basic *mammalian* body plan.
The lab studies *mammalian* cells.
Milk is a *mammalian* invention.

contrast: Also a noun — the extinct elephant.

senses.gloss: Enormous.
examples: Rebuilding the bridge is a *mammoth* undertaking.
The company posted a *mammoth* loss last quarter.
They hauled in a *mammoth* Christmas tree.

senses.gloss: Made by people rather than occurring in nature.
examples: The lake is *man-made*.
Nylon is a *man-made* fiber.
The famine was *man-made*, not the result of drought.

contrast: The same form works as an adverb: *they played man-to-man all night*.

senses.gloss: Of a talk: frank and direct between two men.
examples: His dad sat him down for a *man-to-man* talk.
What they needed was a *man-to-man* conversation, not another email.

senses.gloss: In sports, with each player guarding one opponent.
examples: The coach switched to a *man-to-man* defense in the fourth quarter.
They lost because their *man-to-man* coverage broke down.

senses.gloss: Small or simple enough to deal with.
examples: Break the project into *manageable* pieces.
The debt is large but still *manageable*.
Short hair is more *manageable* in the summer.

senses.gloss: Of managers or the work of managing.
examples: She moved into a *managerial* role after five years on the floor.
The job calls for *managerial* experience.
It was a *managerial* decision, not a technical one.

senses.gloss: Required by a rule or a law.
examples: Helmets are *mandatory* for all riders.
The training is *mandatory*, not a suggestion.
The state has a *mandatory* five-day waiting period.

contrast: American spelling *maneuverable*; British writing has *manoeuvrable*.

senses.gloss: Easy to steer and turn.
examples: The little boat is far more *maneuverable* than the ferry.
A short wheelbase makes the truck *maneuverable* in the city.
They wanted a *maneuverable* fighter, not a fast one.

senses.gloss: Badly crushed, torn or twisted out of shape.
examples: A *mangled* bicycle lay under the guardrail.
His hand was *mangled* in the machine.
She read out a *mangled* version of my name.

form: from the noun *mange*, a skin disease of animals

senses.gloss: Of an animal: having mange, with patches of missing fur.
examples: A *mangy* stray dog followed us down the alley.
The fox looked thin and *mangy*.

senses.gloss: Shabby and dirty.
examples: He sat on a *mangy* couch in the corner.
The second motel was even *mangier* than the first.

senses.gloss: Behaving in a wild, crazy way.
examples: He let out a *maniacal* laugh.
There was a *maniacal* gleam in her eye.
The pace in the kitchen was close to *maniacal*.

senses.gloss: Full of wild, restless energy.
examples: December is *manic* at the post office.
He gets a little *manic* before a deadline.

senses.gloss: In medicine, of the excited phase of bipolar disorder.
examples: The drug controls her *manic* episodes.
A *manic* phase can last for weeks.

contrast: Doctors now say *bipolar*; *manic-depressive* is the older term you still meet in books.

senses.gloss: Swinging between wild highs and deep lows of mood.
examples: He was diagnosed as *manic-depressive* in his twenties.
The memoir describes a *manic-depressive* year in painful detail.
Her moods that spring were almost *manic-depressive*.

contrast: Formal. Also a verb (*to manifest itself*) and a noun (a ship's *manifest*), both spelled the same.

senses.gloss: Plain to see, needing no proof.
examples: His impatience was *manifest* to everyone in the room.
The report describes a *manifest* failure of oversight.
Their joy became *manifest* the moment the doors opened.

contrast: Formal and literary; everyday English says *many*. Also a noun — the pipe on a car engine.

senses.gloss: Many and of many kinds.
examples: The benefits of the treaty were *manifold*.
She listed the *manifold* problems with the design.
His talents are *manifold*.

senses.gloss: Controlling people by clever, dishonest means.
examples: Her ex was charming and deeply *manipulative*.
The ad is *manipulative*, and children can't see through it.
He uses guilt in a *manipulative* way.

form: *man* + -ly — here -ly makes an adjective, not an adverb

senses.gloss: Having the qualities people expect of a man, such as strength or courage.
examples: He thought crying wasn't *manly*.
She admired his quiet, *manly* patience.
No sport looked *manlier* to him than boxing.

contrast: NASA now writes *crewed*, but *manned* is still everywhere in older texts.

senses.gloss: Having people on board or on duty.
examples: The first *manned* flight to the Moon left in 1969.
There is a *manned* guard post at the gate.
They compared *manned* and unmanned missions.

contrast: Also a noun — the book of instructions.

senses.gloss: Worked by hand rather than automatically.
examples: The car has a *manual* transmission.
Switch the camera to *manual* focus.

senses.gloss: Of work done with the hands and the body.
examples: He spent twenty years in *manual* labor.
The town lost most of its *manual* jobs when the mill closed.

senses.gloss: Made in a factory, usually in quantity.
examples: *Manufactured* goods make up most of the country's exports.
They live in a *manufactured* home outside town.

senses.gloss: Created on purpose to look real when it is not.
examples: The scandal was pure *manufactured* outrage.
Critics called the shortage a *manufactured* crisis.

contrast: Capitalized, and *a Maoist* is also a noun.

senses.gloss: Following the communist ideas of Mao Zedong.
examples: A *Maoist* faction controlled the countryside for a decade.
He wrote a history of *Maoist* economic policy.
Her politics in college were frankly *Maoist*.

senses.gloss: Roaming around looking for things to steal or destroy.
examples: *Marauding* bands burned three villages that winter.
Farmers lost half the crop to *marauding* elk.
The town built its wall against *marauding* raiders.

senses.gloss: Streaked with lines of another color, the way marble is.
examples: A well *marbled* steak stays juicy on the grill.
The book has *marbled* endpapers in blue and gold.
The soap came out *marbled* green and white.

senses.gloss: So small that it hardly matters.
examples: The new engine gave only a *marginal* gain in mileage.
Her influence on the decision was *marginal*.

senses.gloss: At the edge of a group or an area, and not part of the center.
examples: The party was a *marginal* force until the last election.
Wheat grows poorly on this *marginal* land.

contrast: Capitalized, *a Marine* is a noun — a member of the Marine Corps.

senses.gloss: Living in or belonging to the sea.
examples: She studies *marine* mammals off the coast of Maine.
Plastic is choking *marine* life.

senses.gloss: Having to do with ships and shipping.
examples: The cargo is covered by *marine* insurance.
He runs a *marine* supply store at the harbor.

contrast: Don't mix up *marital* (of marriage) with *martial* (of war) — the letters are nearly the same.

senses.gloss: Of marriage or of husband and wife.
examples: The form asks for your *marital* status.
They went through years of *marital* trouble.
The state divides *marital* property evenly.

senses.gloss: Connected with the sea, ships and sailing.
examples: The museum tells the city's *maritime* history.
Two navies patrol the *maritime* border.

senses.gloss: Near the sea, or typical of places near it.
examples: The island has a mild *maritime* climate.
He grew up in a small *maritime* town.

contrast: The adverb *markedly* gains a syllable: MAHR-kid-lee.

senses.gloss: Clear enough that anyone would notice it.
examples: There has been a *marked* improvement since March.
She spoke with a *marked* Southern accent.

senses.gloss: Singled out, usually for harm.
examples: After testifying he was a *marked* man.
The informant knew he was *marked*.

senses.gloss: Easy to sell, or likely to find buyers.
examples: Coding is a *marketable* skill in almost any town.
The house needs paint before it will be *marketable*.
He picked a degree he thought was more *marketable*.

senses.gloss: Left in a place you cannot get away from.
examples: The sailors were *marooned* on a bare island for nine months.
We were *marooned* in the airport all night.
The flood left a dozen *marooned* families on their roofs.

senses.gloss: Spoiled by something that damages it.
examples: The ceremony was *marred* by a sudden storm.
He ran his hand over the *marred* surface of the desk.
Her record is *marred* by one bad season.

senses.gloss: Wet and soft, like a marsh.
examples: The ground near the creek is *marshy* all spring.
They lost a boot crossing the *marshy* field.
The far end of the meadow is *marshier* than this one.

contrast: Don't mix up *martial* (of war) with *marital* (of marriage).

senses.gloss: Of war, soldiers or fighting.
examples: The country has been under *martial* law since June.
She has studied *martial* arts since she was six.
The band struck up a *martial* tune.

contrast: Capitalized. Also a noun — *a Martian*.

senses.gloss: Of the planet Mars.
examples: The rover sent back photos of the *Martian* surface.
A *Martian* day is about forty minutes longer than ours.
The film opens with a *Martian* dust storm.

contrast: American spelling *marvelous*, with one l; British writing has *marvellous*.

senses.gloss: Extremely good or pleasing.
examples: We had a *marvelous* time in Chicago.
She is a *marvelous* cook.
The weather that week was simply *marvelous*.

contrast: Capitalized, and also a noun — *she is a Marxist*.

senses.gloss: Following the political and economic ideas of Karl Marx.
examples: He teaches a course on *Marxist* theory.
The paper takes a *Marxist* view of the strike.
Two of the parties in the coalition are openly *Marxist*.

contrast: *Masculine* is about qualities and style; *male* is about biological sex.

senses.gloss: Having qualities or a look traditionally thought of as belonging to men.
examples: The room is dark and heavily *masculine*.
He has a deep, *masculine* voice.

senses.gloss: In grammar, belonging to the gender that goes with words like *he*.
examples: In Spanish, *libro* is *masculine*.
German has *masculine*, feminine and neuter nouns.

senses.gloss: Wearing a mask.
examples: Two *masked* men walked into the bank.
Guests arrived for a *masked* ball.

senses.gloss: Hidden behind something that covers it up.
examples: Painkillers can leave *masked* symptoms that fool the doctor.
Under the compliment was a *masked* threat.

senses.gloss: Seeming to enjoy pain or suffering, your own most of all.
examples: Running a marathon in August is a little *masochistic*.
He has a *masochistic* habit of rereading his bad reviews.
Staying in that job was plainly *masochistic*.

contrast: Capitalized; it belongs to the Freemasons, not to stonework.

senses.gloss: Of the Freemasons.
examples: The meeting was held in the old *Masonic* temple.
He wore a ring with a *Masonic* symbol.
The town's *Masonic* lodge dates from 1870.

contrast: Also a noun (*a mass of people*) and, capitalized, the church service.

senses.gloss: Involving or aimed at very large numbers of people.
examples: Television is still the great *mass* medium.
The factory turned to *mass* production in 1913.
There was a *mass* evacuation of the coast.

senses.gloss: Made in large numbers by machine, all copies alike.
examples: The chairs are *mass-produced* and cost twelve dollars each.
He hates *mass-produced* furniture.
Once the vaccine was *mass-produced*, the price fell.

senses.gloss: Very large and heavy.
examples: A *massive* oak door closed behind us.
The bridge rests on two *massive* concrete piers.

senses.gloss: Very great in amount or degree.
examples: He suffered a *massive* heart attack.
The campaign raised a *massive* amount of money.

contrast: *Masterful* now covers both skill and command; *masterly* means skill only.

senses.gloss: Done with great skill.
examples: It was a *masterful* piece of editing.
Her handling of the reporters was *masterful*.

senses.gloss: Used to giving orders and expecting them to be obeyed.
examples: He took the wheel in a *masterful* way that annoyed everyone.
Her voice turned *masterful* the moment the crew arrived.

senses.gloss: Fitting or equal to something else, so the two go together.
examples: The two fighters were evenly *matched*.
She brought out a set of *matched* silver candlesticks.
Badly *matched* tires wear out fast.

senses.gloss: Of the same color, pattern or kind as something else.
examples: She wore a green dress and a *matching* hat.
The twins showed up in *matching* sweaters.
The company offers a *matching* contribution to your savings.

contrast: Also a noun — cloth, or the stuff something is made of.

senses.gloss: Of physical things, money and possessions rather than the mind or spirit.
examples: They have every *material* comfort and still aren't happy.
The scholarship covers her *material* needs.

senses.gloss: Important enough to affect the outcome.
examples: The witness had no *material* evidence to offer.
That detail is not *material* to the case.

senses.gloss: Caring too much about money and possessions.
examples: He calls the whole holiday shallow and *materialistic*.
She grew less *materialistic* after the move.
It was a *materialistic* decade, and the ads showed it.

senses.gloss: Of a mother, or like a mother.
examples: She felt a sudden *maternal* urge to protect him.
The hospital tracks *maternal* health for a year after birth.

senses.gloss: Related to you through your mother.
examples: My *maternal* grandfather came from Naples.
The gene came down the *maternal* line.

senses.gloss: Of mathematics, or done with numbers and calculation.
examples: The proof rests on a simple *mathematical* argument.
He has real *mathematical* ability.
Their chance of winning is a *mathematical* certainty now.

senses.gloss: Ruled or led by women, especially by mothers.
examples: Elephant herds are *matriarchal*.
She studies a *matriarchal* society in southern China.
The family is quietly *matriarchal*: grandma decides everything.

contrast: Formal and legal; in everyday speech people say *marriage* as a modifier or *marital*.

senses.gloss: Of marriage or of the wedding.
examples: The lawyer handles *matrimonial* cases.
They signed a *matrimonial* agreement before the wedding.
The paper still runs *matrimonial* ads.

form: *matron* + -ly — here -ly makes an adjective, not an adverb

senses.gloss: Of a middle-aged woman: plump, settled and rather old-fashioned.
examples: A *matronly* woman in a flowered dress took our tickets.
She thought the coat made her look *matronly*.
He remembered her as *matronly* and endlessly kind.

contrast: Spelled *matte* but pronounced exactly like *mat*.

senses.gloss: Dull rather than shiny.
examples: We painted the ceiling a flat *matte* white.
She prefers a *matte* lipstick.
Print the photos *matte*, not glossy.

senses.gloss: Stuck together in a thick, tangled mass.
examples: The dog's fur was *matted* with mud.
His hair lay *matted* against his forehead.
We pulled up a layer of *matted* leaves.

form: compound — a whole phrase used as one adjective

senses.gloss: Saying something calmly, as plain fact, with no feeling shown.
examples: She announced the diagnosis in a *matter-of-fact* voice.
He was surprisingly *matter-of-fact* about losing the house.
The report is short and *matter-of-fact*.

comparison: -er/-est or more/most — *maturer* or *more mature*, *maturest* or *most mature*

senses.gloss: Grown up, and sensible in the way adults are expected to be.
examples: She is very *mature* for fourteen.
His brother is three years older but no *more mature*.

senses.gloss: Fully grown or fully developed.
examples: The yard has two *mature* maples.
The cheese is aged until it is *mature*.

senses.gloss: Sentimental and tearful in a silly way, often after drinking.
examples: After the third beer he turned *maudlin* about his college years.
The song is *maudlin*, but the crowd loves it.
She cut the speech before it got *maudlin*.

senses.gloss: Of a pale purple color.
examples: The bridesmaids wore *mauve*.
She chose a *mauve* wallpaper for the hall.
The sky went *mauve* just after sunset.

contrast: Also a noun: *he's a maverick*.

senses.gloss: Refusing to follow the group and doing things your own way.
examples: A *maverick* senator broke with her party on the vote.
He built the company with a *maverick* streak and a lot of luck.
The film follows a *maverick* detective who ignores every rule.

contrast: Also a noun: *a maximum of ten people*.

senses.gloss: The greatest that is possible or allowed.
examples: The *maximum* speed on this road is 55.
He got the *maximum* sentence.
Set the oven to its *maximum* temperature.

senses.gloss: Of a mayor or a mayor's office.
examples: The *mayoral* race drew nine candidates.
She announced her *mayoral* campaign in March.
The *mayoral* term here is four years.

contrast: American spelling *meager*; British writing has *meagre*.

senses.gloss: Much too small in amount.
examples: They lived on his *meager* pension.
The results after six months were *meager*.
Dinner was a *meager* bowl of soup.

senses.gloss: Afraid to say plainly what you mean.
examples: Don't be *mealy-mouthed* — tell them the project failed.
The statement was a *mealy-mouthed* non-apology.
Voters are tired of *mealy-mouthed* answers.

senses.gloss: Following a long, winding course.
examples: A *meandering* creek cuts through the pasture.
We took the *meandering* coast road instead of the highway.

senses.gloss: Going on and on without getting to the point.
examples: He gave a *meandering* answer that lasted ten minutes.
The novel's *meandering* middle section loses most readers.

senses.gloss: Serious and important, worth doing or having.
examples: She wanted *meaningful* work, not another spreadsheet.
There has been no *meaningful* progress since July.

senses.gloss: Of a look or a pause: carrying a message that is not said out loud.
examples: He gave his wife a *meaningful* glance across the table.
There was a *meaningful* silence after the question.

senses.gloss: Having no meaning, purpose or value.
examples: Without enforcement the rule is *meaningless*.
He filled the page with *meaningless* jargon.
The last game of the season was *meaningless* for both teams.

contrast: Informal, and always a complaint about how small something is.

senses.gloss: Annoyingly small in amount.
examples: All that work for a *measly* twelve dollars.
They gave us a *measly* two days' notice.
He left a *measly* tip on a hundred-dollar check.

senses.gloss: Big enough to be measured or clearly noticed.
examples: The program produced a *measurable* drop in absences.
Set goals that are *measurable*.
There was no *measurable* rainfall all month.

senses.gloss: Careful and controlled, not rushed or angry.
examples: The governor gave a *measured* response to the attack.
He answered in a *measured* tone.

senses.gloss: Slow and regular in rhythm.
examples: We heard the *measured* tread of boots on the stairs.
She read the poem at a *measured* pace.

senses.gloss: Living on meat.
examples: *Meat-eating* dinosaurs walked on two legs.
The pitcher plant is the garden's one *meat-eating* resident.
She cooks for a house of *meat-eating* teenagers.

senses.gloss: Containing no meat.
examples: The diner has a *meatless* chili on Fridays.
We try to have two *meatless* days a week.
She brought a *meatless* lasagna to the potluck.
